title: The Lamp
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Lamp, well filled with oil, burned with a clear and steady light, and began to swell with pride and boast that it shone more brightly than the sun himself. Just then a puff of wind came and blew it out. Some one struck a match and lit it again, and said, "You just keep alight, and never mind the sun. Why, even the stars never need to be relit as you had to be just now."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what kind of light does the well-filled Lamp burn with?
options: A dim and flickering light
A bright but uneven light
A clear and steady light
A colorful, changing light

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Lamp boast about itself?
options: That it shone more brightly than the sun himself
That it never needed to be refilled with oil
That it could burn forever without going out
That it was more beautiful than any star

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happens to the Lamp right after its boast?
options: It runs out of oil suddenly
It grows even brighter than before
It is knocked over by someone passing by
A puff of wind blows it out

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does someone do after the Lamp goes out?
options: They throw the Lamp away
They strike a match and light it again
They add more oil before relighting it
They leave it dark for the rest of the night

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the person say the Lamp should never mind?
options: The wind
The stars
The sun
The match

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the person point out about the stars?
options: They never need to be relit
They shine brighter than the Lamp
They go out every single night
They are jealous of the Lamp's light

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why is the Lamp's boast shown to be foolish so quickly?
options: The sun immediately grows brighter to prove the Lamp wrong
The Lamp runs out of oil moments after boasting
Another lamp nearby challenges its claim directly
A single puff of wind is enough to extinguish it entirely, unlike the sun or stars

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what point does comparing the Lamp to the stars make about its claim to outshine the sun?
options: The stars are actually dimmer than the Lamp in every way
Even ordinary stars are more reliable and enduring than the boastful Lamp
The Lamp is more valuable than the stars because it can be relit
The comparison to stars has nothing to do with the Lamp's boast

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "swell with pride" mean in the passage?
options: To physically grow larger in size
To become suddenly dim and weak
To become filled with an excessive sense of one's own importance
To make a loud, boastful noise

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Boasting about your own brilliance can be quickly undone by how easily you can be extinguished
Lamps are more reliable sources of light than the sun
Wind is the greatest danger any light source can face
Stars are inferior to any light made by humans

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what condition is the Lamp in at the very start?
options: Nearly empty of oil
Freshly cleaned and polished
Recently repaired after breaking
Well filled with oil

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what tool does someone use to relight the Lamp?
options: A candle
A match
Another lamp
A piece of flint

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the person tell the Lamp to keep doing?
options: Shine brighter each night
Compare itself to the stars
Stay alight
Warn others about the wind

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might the timing of the wind gust be considered ironic?
options: It extinguishes the Lamp at the very moment it claims to outshine the sun
It happens long after the Lamp has stopped boasting
It only affects the sun, not the Lamp itself
It causes the Lamp to burn even brighter than before

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does needing to be relit reveal about the Lamp's true strength compared to its boast?
options: Its light is actually stronger than the sun's after being relit
Its light needs no outside help at all to keep burning
Its light was never really extinguished in the first place
Its light is fragile and dependent on outside help, unlike what it claimed

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "relit" mean in "never need to be relit"?
options: Cleaned and polished
Lit again after going out
Moved to a new location
Replaced with a new one

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Lamp successfully outshines the sun for one night
A Lamp is replaced permanently after going out
A boastful Lamp is blown out by the wind and reminded that even the stars outlast it
The wind and the Lamp become rivals for the rest of the story
